OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Amodei to brief UNSC as France flags AI threat to kids, global security

Meeting called by Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot because AI's security implications had not received enough attention at the Security Council, says a French official.

Debdutta Chakraborty

23 September, 2026 03:54 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

France's President Emmanuel Macron addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, the US | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: France is convening a high-level meeting at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) on Wednesday in which OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face CEOs will brief the 15-member council on the risks posed by artificial intelligence.

France holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for September, coinciding with the opening of the 81st Session of the General Assembly in New York.

A French official said the meeting had been called by Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot because the security implications of artificial intelligence had not received enough attention at the Security Council.

Show Full Article

“We consider that artificial intelligence and the threat it could cause has not been sufficiently discussed, especially at the Security Council, and this is why Minister Barrault called for this meeting,” the official said at a media briefing.

French President Emmanuel Macron is expected to host an event focused on protecting children from potential harms associated with artificial intelligence. The initiative brings together governments, technology companies, civil society organisations and foundations, with the stated goal of ensuring that AI benefits children without harming their cognitive and social development.

About 20 countries are expected to participate at various levels, including heads of state and ministers, according to officials.

“The French president will have a major event on the protection of children with AI, which is a coalition bringing together governments, companies, civil society organisations, foundations, with a focus on ensuring that the development of AI benefits our children and do not harm their cognitive and social development, which is a key topic for the future of our society,” the French official added.

The Security Council meeting will address a different set of concerns. “AI has reached a level of development where it raises questions for global security,” the official said. “Now, on several fronts, the malicious use of models, but also the risk of losing control over advanced models, or autonomous weapons, for instance.”

The decision to invite the technology companies directly involved in developing advanced AI systems reflects the growing role of private companies in shaping the technology and its associated risks.

The official added that OpenAI was invited “in light of the recent security incident of this summer,” where independent AI test agents broke out of their sandboxes and accessed external systems, while Anthropic would appear “in light of its proposal on basing the development of advanced AI systems”.

According to the French officials, governments would ultimately have to establish the rules governing the technology and it will be discussed in the UNSC meeting.

The Security Council has previously addressed emerging technologies in the context of international peace and security, but the French initiative puts the rapidly evolving capabilities of generative and advanced AI systems directly before the council.

The first briefer will be Joshua Bengio, co-chair of the International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, who is expected to offer what the official described as “an independent academic perspective on the threats that AI causes to peace and security”.

He will be followed by Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, and Clément Delangue, the chief executive and co-founder of Hugging Face, the French artificial intelligence company.

Another French official said Paris believed the technology offered substantial benefits but also required international safeguards.

“First, by saying that France has put AI very firmly on the agenda of this UN General Assembly, and that was on purpose because AI is playing an increasingly important role around the world, no need to say about it,” the official added.

“We strongly believe in the immense benefits it could have, but it has to be done well.”

In the UN General Assembly’s 81st session Tuesday, France President Emmanuel Macron had also focused on the risks posed by AI, particularly the fact that most people and countries have little or no say in the debate over how the technology should be regulated.

He argued that decisions about AI should not be left solely to the US, China and a small group of private companies. The stakes, he said, were too high, given that the technology could threaten “the security of our States, of our hospitals, of our banks”.

“We must defend science. We have waited too long to protect our children and adolescents from social media. Everywhere in our societies, we see the consequences,” Macron said.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

What China’s state media is saying ahead of Xi-Trump Summit

China's state-run Global Times has laid out Beijing's case for a more predictable US-China relationship. Here's what China wants from the Xi-Trump meeting.

Raunaq Lekhi

23 September, 2026 03:08 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Donald Trump greets Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, on Oct. 30, 2025. | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Chinese President Xi Jinping is in the US for a state visit that Beijing is portraying as an opportunity to put a more stable footing under its increasingly complicated relationship with Washington.

Xi, who is visiting the US from 23-25 September at the invitation of US President Donald Trump, will meet the American president just four months after Trump’s state visit to China in May. The two leaders had then agreed to work towards what they called a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”.

In the past two days, China’s state-run Global Times has repeatedly returned to that phrase, describing the latest Xi-Trump meeting as an attempt to give greater predictability to ties between the world’s two largest economies.

Show Full Article

But what does Beijing appear to want from the meeting?

Stability, without ending competition The Global Times’ coverage in the run up to the meeting suggests China is not presenting stability as the end of rivalry between Beijing and Washington.

An editorial published ahead of Xi’s visit described the proposed relationship as one where cooperation remains possible alongside competition and differences. Another commentary broke the idea down into four principles: cooperation as the mainstay, competition within limits, managing differences through dialogue and maintaining peace.

That distinction is important because trade, technology and security remain major sources of friction between the two countries.

The message from Beijing, as reflected in the Global Times coverage, is therefore less about resolving every disagreement and more about preventing those disagreements from destabilising the wider relationship.

Read Here: World keeps pushing Russia, India, China together. Then RIC tears itself apart

Trade and technology are key Economic ties feature prominently in the coverage.

Chinese and US officials held economic and trade consultations ahead of Xi’s visit, discussing bilateral trade and investment as well as artificial intelligence. Global Times quoted Chinese experts as saying continued talks were necessary to implement earlier agreements and reduce trade friction

Veteran US diplomat Chas W. Freeman Jr, who served as an interpreter during former US president Richard Nixon’s 1972 China visit, told Global Times that both countries should concentrate on areas where their interests overlap.

He pointed to trade, climate change, nuclear non-proliferation and management of the global economy as areas where cooperation remains possible despite ideological and political differences. Freeman also argued that the two countries should stop trying to hold back each other’s development and instead compete by becoming more competitive themselves.

AI is another emerging area. Global Times reported that the two sides discussed AI during their latest economic consultations, while one US academic interviewed by the newspaper said cooperation on AI governance could be an area where Beijing and Washington work together.

Why keep talking when tensions remain? One argument running through the recent coverage is that regular contact itself has value.

Freeman told Global Times that losing contact could deepen mutual suspicion and eventually turn it into hostility. He argued that the two countries need to rediscover the logic behind the 1972 Shanghai Communiqué: China and the US have different political and socioeconomic systems, but can still cooperate where their interests overlap.

Global Times has also highlighted people-to-people exchanges, including American students travelling to China and Chinese and US businesses expanding into each other’s markets.

An editorial published Wednesday pointed to Chinese bubble-tea brands operating in the US and American fast-food chains expanding in China as examples of what it described as “everyday” connections between the two societies.

What could come out of the meeting? The recent Global Times coverage does not point to a single expected breakthrough. Instead, it stresses incremental progress: keeping trade relations stable, expanding practical cooperation, managing disputes and maintaining regular communication between the two governments.

That does not mean the major disagreements have disappeared. Global Times itself noted that stability does not remove the problems between Beijing and Washington, while another commentary identified Taiwan as a major underlying variable in the relationship.

The broader message from the coverage is therefore relatively straightforward: Beijing wants the Xi-Trump meeting to reinforce the framework agreed by the two leaders in May – competition without uncontrolled confrontation, cooperation where interests overlap, and dialogue when differences persist.

Whether that produces concrete agreements will depend on what Xi and Trump are able to achieve at the table.

Economic activity regains momentum in September after slump, survey shows

Indian economy proved more resilient than expected to a war-led energy shock, expanding 7.8% last quarter as household consumption & business investment-powered growth.

Anup Roy

23 September, 2026 01:10 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Market stalls in Mumbai, India. Photographer: Abeer Khan/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

India’s economic activity accelerated in September, regaining momentum after slowing in recent months as manufacturing climbed to seven-month high and services picked up pace, a flash survey by HSBC Holdings Plc showed Wednesday.

The services purchasing managers’ index rose to 55.8 from 54.1 in August, while the manufacturing purchasing managers’ climbed rose to 55.7 from 52.8 last month. That left the composite index at 56.5, compared with 54.3 in August.

The indexes, which provide an early gauge of private-sector activity, are based on preliminary survey responses and may be revised when final PMI figures are released next month. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below that level signals contraction.

Show Full Article

“Output growth ticked higher at both manufacturing and services companies, with goods producers leading the latest upturn. Aggregate new orders also rose at a quicker pace, prompting a solid expansion in jobs,” HSBC said in a statement. With the expansion in place, the composite index “was back above its long-run average,” it said.

Bond yields and rupee, however, stayed unchanged after the reading.

India’s economy proved more resilient than expected to a war-led energy shock, expanding 7.8% last quarter as household consumption and business investment powered growth. India, the world’s third-largest oil importer, remains vulnerable to elevated energy costs and supply disruptions that can weigh on domestic activity.

“Renewed tensions in the Middle East have once again led firms to build buffers to manage the uncertainties,” said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC.

Brent crude is hovering around $100 a barrel. However, the government hasn’t raised pump prices since May, insulating the economy from volatile energy prices for now.

Still, price pressures are building. Figures last week showed India’s inflation accelerated in August, moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range and potentially narrowing the scope for policymakers to remain on hold for long.

Most economists expect the Reserve Bank to raise interest rates on Oct. 7. The central bank has stayed on hold so far this year.

Trump says AI is now ‘super intelligence’. Why the new name matters

Trump wants to replace 'artificial intelligence' with 'super intelligence'. But the term already has a specific meaning in the tech world.

Raunaq Lekhi

23 September, 2026 01:06 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

US President Donald Trump speaks during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. The theme of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all." | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald Trump wants to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence”, saying the word “artificial” makes the technology sound fake.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump said US government documents would henceforth use “super intelligence” or “SI” instead of artificial intelligence, and suggested other countries to follow suit.

The proposed name, however, is unlikely to change how researchers or the industry understand the technology. In fact, “super intelligence” already has a specific meaning in discussions about the future of AI.

Show Full Article

What does ‘super intelligence’ actually mean? Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems capable of performing tasks associated with human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising patterns, generating content and solving problems.

“Super intelligence” means something much more specific.

The term is generally used to describe a hypothetical form of AI whose intellectual abilities surpass those of humans across a wide range of areas. It is associated with discussions about AI systems that could potentially reason, learn and solve problems at a level beyond human capability.

That is different from simply giving today’s AI systems a new name.

Researchers have therefore questioned Trump’s use of “super intelligence” to describe existing AI. Experts cited by the BBC said the term is generally reserved for a much more advanced stage of AI, which does not currently exist.

In other words, “super intelligence” is not simply a more accurate synonym for artificial intelligence. It describes a possible future development of the technology.

Read Here: Xi unlikely to take along any CEOs to US summit with Trump

Why does Trump want to rename AI? Trump’s argument is largely about the word “artificial”. He has said it makes intelligence “sound fake”, while arguing that the technology is real and increasingly capable.

The proposed change also fits into his broader approach to AI. Last week, Trump announced plans for an “AI Force” and said he would name an “AI czar” to oversee the industry. He has also pushed back against calls for tighter controls on AI, arguing that the US cannot afford to slow development while competing with China.

At the UN, Trump said the US would not “stifle the growth” of AI, which he described as a technology that could become bigger than the Industrial Revolution. He also dismissed warnings about AI posing an existential threat to humanity as a “hoax”.

His administration’s proposed terminology, however, does not change what AI is.

What other names were considered? Trump had floated several alternatives on his Truth Social platform before settling on “super intelligence”.

Among the names discussed were “superior intelligence”, “extreme intelligence” and “supreme intelligence”. He later used polls on Truth Social to ask followers to weigh in, with “super intelligence” emerging as his preferred choice.

The terminology has already begun appearing among some people in Trump’s orbit, even as its adoption by the wider technology industry remains uncertain.

The proposed change has also drawn a degree of scepticism outside the US. Canadian AI minister Evan Solomon, when asked about the new name, joked that Canadians were “not enthusiastic” about renaming things, in an apparent reference to Trump’s earlier attempts to rename geographical features.

Will AI actually become ‘SI’? For now, there is little indication that the technology industry is preparing to abandon the term AI.

The phrase “artificial intelligence” has been used for decades and covers a vast range of systems, from recommendation algorithms and chatbots to increasingly capable generative AI models.

“Super intelligence”, meanwhile, remains largely a theoretical concept. Using it for existing systems could therefore blur the distinction between what current AI can do and what researchers believe future systems could potentially achieve.

Whether “SI” becomes part of everyday technology language will depend not only on US government documents but also on whether researchers, companies, and the public begin using it. For now, the industry continues to call it AI.
